lead: The Drinking Man's Diet was popularised by Robert Cameron's 1964 booklet. It restricts carbohydrates while allowing meat, fat and spirits, and it is regarded as a forerunner of later low-carb plans such as Atkins.

Its appearance payoff is fat loss: followers aim to get leaner by cutting carbs, with the draw being that social drinking stays on the menu. Reception at the time was mixed, and nutrition experts of the era criticised it.

paras: Followers count carbohydrates, with the commonly cited figure being about 60 grams a day, and favour meats and fats and low-carb drinks such as spirits instead of beer or sugary mixers.

Nutritionists Jean Mayer and Frederick Stare called the plan unhealthy, and an American Medical Association spokesman said it had no scientific basis. Regular alcohol use carries well-documented health risks, and anyone with a medical condition would be advised by clinicians to seek individual guidance.

angle.text: The plan is a route to fat loss through carbohydrate restriction. Its distinguishing feature is that it tolerates drinking, which proponents saw as making dieting easier to sustain.

lead: The Drinking Man's Diet is a low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet that allows alcohol. It was promoted in a 1964 booklet by the photographer and author Robert Cameron (1911-2009), titled The Drinking Man's Diet: How to Lose Weight with a Minimum of Willpower.[1]

People follow it to lose body fat, and so get leaner and look better, while keeping social drinking. The plan is considered a precursor of the Atkins and Paleolithic diets, and the book reportedly sold over 2.4 million copies in 13 languages.[1]
Contemporary commentary was divided. Time magazine in 1965 called it a mix of wishful thinking, nonsense and some sound advice, and prominent nutritionists criticised it.[1]

paras: The plan centres on meat and fat with strictly limited carbohydrate. A commonly cited summary says it suggests about 60 grams of carbohydrate a day while permitting martinis and similar drinks.[2][1]

Nutritionists Jean Mayer and Frederick Stare described the diet as ridiculous and unhealthy, and Dr. Philip L. White of the American Medical Association said it lacked scientific basis.[1] Supporters pointed to its popularity and its framing as a low-willpower approach.[1]
Lifters on T Nation have mentioned the book when discussing the history of low-carb diets, noting it preceded Atkins by eight years.[2]
No studies found. Research on low-carbohydrate diets in general is extensive, but no trial has tested this plan specifically.

timeline.event: Cameron publishes The Drinking Man's Diet.[1]
